title: The Tao that can be told
word: The Tao that can be told
hook: the Tao that can be spoken is not the eternal Tao; the nameless is the origin (Tao Te Ching 1)
carry: not the one that can be told

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Tao: a way, a road, and the name of a book written, the story says, at a gate. Your line was at the gate.

How would you describe the taste of water to someone who had never had any? Cool, maybe. Wet. Plain. Every word slides off it. Or the smell of rain on a hot sidewalk, or the face of someone you love: you can talk for an hour and still not hand it over. The words point; they don't arrive. The Tao Te Ching opens with a warning like that: what it's about can't be fully told, and the moment you've said it, you've already missed it a little.
screen: `THE TASTE OF WATER.` → `THE WORDS POINT. THEY DON'T ARRIVE.` → `A BOOK THAT BEGINS WITH A WARNING.`

segments.voice: First, the opening line, in James Legge's translation: "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name." In Chinese the line opens with one character used twice, first as a noun and then as a verb: the Tao that can be Tao'd. That character can mean a road, and it can also mean to say. Legge chose the road, a way you can walk; other translators choose the speaking, a way you can tell. The line makes sense either way: any Tao you can map or describe is not the whole of it. Second, the nameless and the named. Thought of as having no name, the chapter says, the Tao is the origin of heaven and earth; thought of as having a name, it is the mother of all things. The nameless is where everything comes from. The named is where people live: kitchens, cities, words for every tree. Third, both are the same. The two come from one source and only get different names as things unfold. The chapter doesn't ask you to throw words away; every name is a small door into something larger than the name. Fourth, the mystery has a gate. The chapter ends by calling the deepest point of this mystery a gate, the way in to all that is subtle and wonderful. The book written at a gate opens with one.
screen: `TRODDEN, OR SPOKEN?` · `THE NAMELESS AND THE NAMED.` · `ONE SOURCE, TWO NAMES.` · `THE MYSTERY HAS A GATE.` · then, large: `NOT THE ONE THAT CAN BE TOLD.`

segments.voice: Look at something ordinary, a cup, a leaf, your own hand, and name it once, quietly. Then keep looking past the name, at the color where the light hits it and the small shadow underneath, letting each new word go. If you pray, you can rest in what can't be named; if not, just stay with what's still there after the words run out.
The Tao that can be told. The opening line of the Tao Te Ching, which says that any way you can tread or tell is not the enduring Tao. Today's word.
screen: `THE TAO THAT CAN BE TOLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not the one that can be told. A person, a mood, a day: each is more than its name. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching return to its opening chapter again and again, and some Taoist teachers treat it as a reminder that every description of the Way falls short of the Way itself.

chat.says: If the Tao can't be told, why does the book keep talking about it?
options: It says no words hold all of it, but every name is a small door into something larger.
Because the first line is a joke, and the rest of the book takes it back.
Because it thinks words are useless, so it talks only to show they fail.
chat.meaning: Chapter one says any Tao you can tell isn't the whole of it, yet it doesn't ask you to throw words away: names are small doors.
